```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
                      fig.height = 4)
library(rcli)
```

A composite leading indicator (CLI) combines series whose cycles turn before
the business cycle. `rcli` follows the OECD system of composite leading
indicators (Gyomai and Guidetti 2012) from the choice of candidates to a
tested composite, and adds the statistical checks recommended in the
literature on leading indicators (Marcellino 2006).

## 1. Candidates and specification

Every workflow starts with a reference series and candidate series at the
same frequency. Here we simulate thirty years of monthly data in which the
truth is known: two series lead by six and three months, one is coincident,
one lags, one is counter-cyclical and two are noise.

```{r data}
sim <- simulate_cycles(seed = 2026)
attr(sim, "truth")
```

The OECD asks for an economic rationale for every component; statistics do
not replace it. `rcli` records it and warns when it is missing.

```{r candidates}
meta <- data.frame(
  name = colnames(sim)[-1],
  rationale = c("early_stage", "rapid_response", "rapid_response",
                "rapid_response", "expectations", "prime_mover",
                "prime_mover")
)
cand <- cli_candidates(sim, reference = "reference", meta = meta)
cand
```

All methodological choices live in one specification object:

```{r spec}
spec <- cli_spec(freq = 12)
spec
```

## 2. The whole workflow in one call

```{r build}
res <- cli_build(cand, spec)
res
```

`cli_build()` extracts the cycles, dates the turning points, classifies every
candidate, aggregates the leading ones and tests the composite. The
classification table shows why each series was kept or rejected:

```{r assessment}
assessment(res)
```

The counter-cyclical series was inverted before it was assessed. Its
direction was read from the cross-correlation within a quarter of the
average reference cycle; a longer window would let the opposite phase of a
regular cycle decide. Where the direction is known from the economic
rationale, declare it in a `sign` column of `meta` (1 or -1), as the OECD
does: leads beyond a quarter of the cycle cannot be told apart from
inversion by the data. The audit log records each iteration of the
selection loop:

```{r audit}
audit_log(res)[, c("iteration", "action", "components", "ccf_lag", "passed")]
```

```{r plot, fig.alt = "Composite and reference cycles with reference contractions shaded"}
plot(res)
```

## 3. Step by step

Every step is also available on its own, so a workflow can stop anywhere —
for example after the classification.

```{r steps}
cyc <- cli_cycles(cand, spec)
cyc$lead_6
tp <- cli_turning_points(cyc, spec)
head(as.data.frame(tp$reference))
cli <- cli_composite(cyc, c("lead_6", "lead_3"), spec, cyc$reference)
cli_validate(cli, cyc$reference, spec)
```

Filters, turning-point rules and aggregation methods are interchangeable
objects:

```{r alternatives}
alt <- update(spec, filter = cf_filter(), aggregator = dynamic_factor())
components(cli_build(cand, alt))
```

## 4. How the classification rules were calibrated

The thresholds were not guessed. The script `data-raw/calibrate_collect.R`
simulates 100 samples for each frequency and three noise levels, classifies
every candidate and compares the class with the truth (run again for 0.6.0,
after the changes to the direction rule and the tests). Two lessons shaped
the defaults:

* the median lead at turning points shrinks towards zero as noise grows,
  whereas the lead of the cross-correlation peak stays unbiased, so the
  cross-correlation lead is the primary lead measure;
* concordance alone lets about one noise series in seventy through; adding
  the Toda-Yamamoto Granger test removes almost all of them at nearly no
  loss of power.

```{r calibration}
acc <- read.csv(system.file("calibration", "accuracy.csv",
                            package = "rcli"))
acc[, c("freq", "noise_sd", "correct.leading", "correct.rejected",
        "false_leading", "overall")]
```

With low or moderate noise most candidates are classified correctly, and
non-leading series are almost never labelled leading. With quarterly data and
strong noise the power to detect leaders falls: thirty years give only 120
observations. Pure-noise series are then also called coincident or lagging
more often (up to about 15 percent), which does no harm to the composite.

The tests behind the criteria allow for the persistence of cycles. Phases
last years, so the usual Newey-West variance made the concordance test reject
independent cycles 11 to 37 percent of the time at the 5 percent level; with
the fixed-b variance of Kiefer and Vogelsang (2005) it rejects 6 to 18
percent (`inst/calibration/test-size.csv`, which also records the size of
the Pesaran-Timmermann test and of the prediction criteria).

## 5. Is the in-sample lead real?

Components are chosen because they led in the sample, so the in-sample lead
overstates the lead to expect later. `cli_selection_bias()` chooses the
components with data up to a cut-off date and measures the lead of that
composite only at later turning points.

```{r bias}
cli_selection_bias(cand, spec, cutoffs = c(2012, 2016))
```

In this simulation the leaders are genuine, so the lead after the cut-off is
as long as before it. With real data a large positive `lead_gap` means the
in-sample lead is mostly a selection effect. Set `oos_cutoffs` in the
specification to run this check inside `cli_build()`.

## 6. Is the composite good enough?

`cli_quality()` turns the validation into a scorecard with a verdict. It
checks three groups of criteria:

* **turning points**: the composite meets every leading criterion used to
  classify candidates;
* **prediction**: out-of-sample probabilities of contraction, each from a
  logit fitted to earlier periods only, have an area under the ROC curve of
  at least 0.7 and a quadratic probability score below that of the naive
  forecast from the same past data, and the Pesaran-Timmermann test finds
  that the composite's direction predicts the later direction of the
  reference. The horizon is fixed in advance (the lower end of
  `target_lead`, 6 months by default), not taken from the composite;
* **out of sample**: after the cut-off dates the composite still leads, and
  the in-sample lead does not exceed the later lead by more than `min_lead`.

The verdict is *good* when all three groups pass, *acceptable* when the
first two groups pass but the out-of-sample check was not run, and *weak*
otherwise.

```{r quality}
res_oos <- cli_build(cand, update(spec, oos_cutoffs = c(2012, 2016)))
cli_quality(res_oos)
```

## 7. Mixed frequencies and variable types

`rcli` works at one frequency, but the data rarely arrive that way: GDP is
quarterly, credit is a monthly stock, exchange rates are daily, some sales
are weekly. `cli_align()` brings them to one frequency with the rule set by
the type of each series (`series_types`): flows are summed, stocks are taken
at the end of the period, averages are averaged. Weekly data are spread over
their days before they are summed into months, so that months of five weeks
do not look larger than months of four. A quarterly reference series is
disaggregated to months with the Denton-Cholette method (or Chow-Lin with a
monthly indicator that is not a candidate); quarterly candidates are
interpolated at the month the OECD uses (central month, or last month for
stocks).

```{r align}
gdp_q <- aggregate(sim[, "reference"], nfrequency = 4, FUN = sum)
weeks <- seq(as.Date("1995-01-02"), as.Date("2024-12-23"), by = "week")
sales <- data.frame(date = weeks,
                    value = 700 * exp(cumsum(rnorm(length(weeks), 0, 0.01))))
x <- cli_align(list(gdp = gdp_q, sim[, -1], sales = sales),
               type = c(gdp = "flow", sales = "flow"), reference = "gdp")
attr(x, "alignment")[c(1, 9), ]
cand_mf <- cli_candidates(x, reference = "gdp",
                          meta = data.frame(name = colnames(x)[-1],
                                            rationale = "early_stage"))
res_mf <- cli_build(cand_mf)
leaders(res_mf)
```

When the reference series was disaggregated, the quality scorecard adds a
line saying that its turning-point dates, and so the lead, are uncertain by
about one month: the monthly path inside each quarter is an estimate.

Data published as one file per indicator, at different frequencies, are
read with `read_cli_series()`: each file has a date column (`2001-01-15`,
`15/01/2001`, `2001-01`, `2001Q1`, `2001S1` or `2001`) and one or more value
columns, and the result goes straight into `cli_align()`.

The source frequency of every series (`series_frequencies`) is detected
from its dates and recorded with the candidates (`cand_mf@meta$frequency`);
`cli_align(frequency = )` checks a declared frequency against the data. A
semiannual or annual series can only be the reference: it is disaggregated
like a quarterly one; with Denton-Cholette (the default) or Chow-Lin every
year (or half-year) is kept exactly, and the scorecard notes that its
turning-point dates are uncertain by about half a source period. A
candidate needs at least quarterly data, since one value a year cannot show
a lead of a few months.

```{r align-annual}
gdp_a <- aggregate(sim[, "reference"], nfrequency = 1, FUN = sum)
x_a <- cli_align(list(gdp = gdp_a, sim[, -1]), type = c(gdp = "flow"),
                 reference = "gdp", frequency = c(gdp = "annual"))
attr(x_a, "alignment")[1, ]
all.equal(as.numeric(aggregate(x_a[, "gdp"], nfrequency = 1, FUN = sum)),
          as.numeric(gdp_a))
```

Moving holidays such as Idulfitri shift through the calendar, so fixed
seasonal factors miss them. `holiday_effect()` turns their dates into
regressors for X-13ARIMA-SEATS (package **seasonal**):

```{r holidays, eval = FALSE}
eid <- holiday_effect(idulfitri_dates(1990, 2030), name = "idulfitri")
spec_sa <- cli_spec(seasonal_adjust = TRUE, holidays = eid)
```

`idulfitri_dates()` gives the dates of the arithmetic Islamic calendar,
which can differ from the official Indonesian dates by a day or two; use
the official dates when you have them.

## 8. The OECD method and the defaults

`oecd_spec()` sets every step as in the OECD system (Gyomai and Guidetti
2012): TRAMO outliers with short forecasts before the filter
(`tramo_outliers()`, through RJDemetra or, without Java, the regARIMA part
of X-13), the TRAMO log/level test (`transform = "test"`), the median-lead
classification with the OECD criteria of cyclical conformity and missed or
extra cycles (`oecd_classifier()`), lag-shifting (`lag_shift = TRUE`) and
the chained average growth of the components (`oecd_aggregate()`).
`cli_presentation()` returns the three OECD forms of any composite:
amplitude adjusted, trend restored and its 12-month rate of change.

```{r oecd, eval = FALSE}
res_oecd <- cli_build(cand, oecd_spec())
tail(cli_presentation(res_oecd))
```

The package defaults differ where the simulations in
`data-raw/compare_oecd.R` showed a gain. Classified with the OECD rule, the
calibration candidates give these rates:

```{r oecd-classification}
cmp <- read.csv(system.file("calibration", "oecd-classification.csv",
                            package = "rcli"))
cmp[cmp$rule != "OECD (min 1 matched)", ]
```

The median lead alone (the rule of rcli 0.5.1, `oecd_classifier(conformity
= FALSE)`) labels a fifth of the non-leading candidates (and up to almost
half of the pure-noise series) leading. With the conformity criteria, the
default since 0.6.0, the OECD rule labels only 2 to 8 percent of the others
leading; it finds as many true leaders with little noise, but 2 to 10
percentage points fewer in noisy data. The default rule of the package
stays at about 1 percent or less, but finds fewer leaders in very noisy
data. The aggregation experiment points the other way at the end of the
sample:

```{r oecd-aggregation}
read.csv(system.file("calibration", "oecd-aggregation.csv",
                     package = "rcli"))
```

The plain mean (`level`), the mean chained at the ragged edge (`chain`, the
default since 0.2.0) and the full OECD chain (`oecd`) are identical in
sample, but when the longest-lead component misses its last two values both
chained forms stay much closer to the full-information composite.
Lag-shifting makes the leads slightly more consistent and the composite
misses fewer turning points, but it shortens the lead of the composite by
about three months, to the shortest lead of the components; it is
therefore off by default.

Two OECD ideas became defaults in rcli 0.2.0 after a real-time study
(`data-raw/realtime_defaults.R`): chaining at the ragged edge
(`equal_weight()`, chained only after the last date at which all
components are observed, so that a component that starts late changes
nothing) and extending each series with one year of forecasts before the
filter (`ar_extension()`, an autoregression of the changes instead of
TRAMO, which needs no other software and did as well). The table compares
the last value of pseudo real-time composites with the full-sample
composite:

```{r realtime-defaults}
read.csv(system.file("calibration", "realtime-defaults.csv",
                     package = "rcli"))
```

Chaining makes the direction of the last change right more often; the
extension makes the revision of the last value smaller; 0.2.0 has both. The
classification is hardly affected (section 4 shows the thresholds
recalibrated with the extension), so the thresholds were kept. To reproduce
rcli 0.1.x:

```{r old-defaults, eval = FALSE}
cli_spec(aggregator = equal_weight(ragged_edge = "level"),
         extension = no_extension())
```

TRAMO-type outliers and the robust default classify the candidates
equally well when spikes and a level shift are injected:

```{r oecd-outliers}
read.csv(system.file("calibration", "oecd-outliers.csv", package = "rcli"))
```

## 9. A coincident index

A coincident index summarises where the cycle is now. The Conference Board
publishes one next to its leading index, and it is the natural monthly
reference when the reference series is quarterly GDP. `cci_build()`
aggregates the candidates that `cli_assess()` classified as coincident,
with the same aggregator as the leading composite, and tests the index for
timing instead of lead. Here two of the simulated series are truly
coincident.

```{r cci}
sim_c <- simulate_cycles(
  leads = c(lead_6 = 6, lead_3 = 3, coin_a = 0, coin_b = 0, lag_3 = -3),
  seed = 2026
)
meta_c <- data.frame(name = colnames(sim_c)[-1], rationale = "rapid_response")
res_c <- cli_build(cli_candidates(sim_c, "reference", meta = meta_c))
cci <- cci_build(res_c)
cci
cli_quality(cci)
```

The criteria mirror the leading ones: a cross-correlation peak within
`coincident_band` of lag 0, a median lead at turning points within
+/- 2 months (one quarter for quarterly data), few missed and extra turning
points and significant concordance (`coincident_criteria()`). Granger
causality is not required, and the prediction group scores the current
contraction state. In the simulations the default rule passes 96 to 99
percent of composites of coincident series and at most 1 percent of those
that lead or lag by 3 months at the default noise level; with twice the
noise it errs more often, above all for quarterly data:

```{r cci-calibration}
read.csv(system.file("calibration", "coincident.csv", package = "rcli"))
```

```{r cci-plot}
plot(cci)
```

`cci_as_reference()` makes the index the reference series of a new
candidate set, without the former reference and without the components of
the index, and the leading composite is then built against it:

```{r cci-reference}
cand_c <- cci_as_reference(cci)
leaders(cli_build(cand_c))
```

## 10. Graphical interface

`run_app()` opens a Shiny application (package **shiny**) that walks
through the same ten steps — data, candidate metadata, specification,
cycles, turning points, classification, composite, validation with the
scorecard, coincident index, and export. Each step unlocks the next;
re-running a step clears the results that depend on it. The coincident
index needs only the classification, so rebuilding the composite keeps it.
The export step offers the composite, the classification, the audit log,
the scorecards, the coincident index, the `CliResult` object and an R
script that reproduces the analysis.

```{r app, eval = FALSE}
run_app()               # Indonesian interface
run_app(language = "en")
```

## 11. Extending rcli

A new filter is a subclass of `CycleFilter` with a method for
`extract_cycle()`:

```{r extend}
setClass("FirstDifference", contains = "CycleFilter")
setMethod("extract_cycle", "FirstDifference", function(filter, x, ...) {
  ts(c(NA, diff(as.numeric(x))), start = start(x), frequency = frequency(x))
})
fd <- new("FirstDifference", label = "first difference")
head(extract_cycle(fd, sim[, "lead_6"]))
```

New aggregation methods work the same way with `Aggregator` and
`aggregate_components()`.

Statistics*, 80(1), 45–61.

Indicators*. OECD Publishing, Paris.

Kiefer, N. M. and Vogelsang, T. J. (2005). A new asymptotic theory for
heteroskedasticity-autocorrelation robust tests. *Econometric Theory*,
21(6), 1130–1164.

Marcellino, M. (2006). Leading indicators. In G. Elliott, C. W. J. Granger and
A. Timmermann (eds.), *Handbook of Economic Forecasting*, Vol. 1, 879–960.
Elsevier.

correlated multicategory variables. *Journal of the American Statistical
Association*, 104(485), 325–337.
